summary: This document adds an optional Cryptographic Authentication TLV that LDP can use to secure its Hello messages. It protects against spoofing and some attacks on the IP header, using an HMAC with a NIST Secure Hash Standard hash.

eli5.summary: Before two routers become friends, they say hello. This RFC adds a secret handshake to that hello so a stranger cannot pretend to be a router.

questions: how does ldp hello hmac work
which hash algorithms does ldp hello authentication use
subtitle: An optional TLV that signs LDP Hello messages with an HMAC so spoofed Hellos can be rejected.

tldr.problem: LDP Hello messages travel over UDP, so TCP security cannot protect them. A spoofed Hello can make a valid adjacency time out or end the LDP session.
tldr.mechanism: A new Cryptographic Authentication TLV (type 0x0405) carries a Security Association ID, a 64-bit strictly increasing sequence number and an HMAC digest computed with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512.
tldr.outcome: Receivers drop Hellos with a bad digest or a non-increasing sequence number. HMAC-SHA-256 is the mandatory default, and the RFC recommends that all deployments use the TLV.

today: RFC 7349 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Security Considerations recommend that all deployments use the Cryptographic Authentication TLV.

sections.title: Why Hellos Need Protecting
sections.content:
LDP peers find and keep track of each other with Hello messages sent in UDP, to the 'all routers on this subnet' address or to a specific IP address. Because they use UDP, they cannot use the TCP security mechanisms such as RFC 5926.

Spoofing is a real problem. A spoofed Hello with a smaller Hold Time can make the receiver expect Hellos more often than the true neighbour sends them, so the adjacency times out. A spoofed Hello with a different Transport Address can end the LDP session directly. RFC 6952 reports that spoofed Hellos have been observed in production networks.

Existing defences are partial. Accepting Hellos only on trusted interfaces, GTSM (RFC 6720) and access lists do not stop packet spoofing or replay. This document adds an optional Cryptographic Authentication TLV that secures the message and a sequence number to resist replay.
sections.eli5: Anyone could shout 'hello, I am your friend' and fool a router. A secret code in the greeting stops that.

sections.title: The Cryptographic Authentication TLV
sections.content:
The TLV is a new Optional Parameter for the Hello message, type 0x0405. Its value holds a 32-bit Security Association ID, a 64-bit Cryptographic Sequence Number and the variable-length Authentication Data. The Length field counts the value, including the SA ID and sequence number.

The sequence number MUST increase for every Hello sent. A receiver MUST drop a Hello whose number is not greater than the last one accepted from that neighbour. It is a single space per LDP router and must stay strictly increasing for the router's deployed life, including cold restarts. One suggested method is to use the high-order 32 bits as a boot count. If the 64-bit number wraps, all keys MUST be reset.

The digest length follows the algorithm: 20 bytes for HMAC-SHA1, 32 for HMAC-SHA-256, 48 for HMAC-SHA-384 and 64 for HMAC-SHA-512. The key itself MUST NOT be carried in the packet.
sections.eli5: The greeting carries a key number, a counter that only goes up so old greetings cannot be replayed, and a scrambled fingerprint of the message.

sections.title: Security Associations and Keys
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters shared by two legitimate LDP speakers: the SA ID, the authentication algorithm, the key, and four times, KeyStartAccept, KeyStartGenerate, KeyStopGenerate and KeyStopAccept. The algorithm is never sent on the wire. The SA ID is configured by the operator and tells the receiver which key and algorithm apply. Different SA IDs can use different algorithms, so new ones can be introduced without breaking sessions.

For smooth key changes, KeyStartAccept SHOULD be earlier than KeyStartGenerate, and KeyStopGenerate SHOULD be earlier than KeyStopAccept. Key storage SHOULD survive restarts. If the last key on an interface expires, the router SHOULD notify the network manager and keep treating the key as valid rather than fall back to no authentication.
sections.eli5: Each pair of routers shares a numbered secret. Keys get start and end times so they can be swapped without anyone being locked out.

sections.title: Computing the HMAC
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256, which is the default, SHOULD support HMAC-SHA-1, and MAY support HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. HMAC is as defined in RFC 2104.

To stop cross-protocol replay between protocols that share keys, the 2-octet LDP Cryptographic Protocol ID is appended to the key. The result is padded with zeros, or hashed if too long, to the hash length. The RFC recommends the key be at least that long.

The sender fills the Authentication Data field with a placeholder called AuthTag (the source IP address followed by the repeated value 0x878FE1F3), then computes the HMAC over the Hello message without the IP and UDP headers. The result replaces AuthTag in the TLV.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix the secret into the message to make a fingerprint. Only someone who knows the secret can make the matching fingerprint.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Hellos
sections.content:
On sending, the router sets the TLV Length by algorithm (24 for HMAC-SHA-1, 36 for HMAC-SHA-256, 52 for HMAC-SHA-384, 68 for HMAC-SHA-512), sets the SA ID, computes the HMAC and stores it.

On receipt, a router that has a stored sequence number for the source address, or is configured to require authentication, MUST discard unauthenticated Hellos. It then finds the SA by ID. If the SA is missing or not valid for reception, the Hello MUST be discarded and an error SHOULD be logged. The same applies if the sequence number is not greater than the last one from that neighbour or if the recomputed digest differs. Logging needs to be rate limited so a storm of spoofed Hellos cannot exhaust resources. After a Hello passes, the router MUST store its sequence number for later replay checks.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the key number, checks the counter is newer, and rebuilds the fingerprint. Any mismatch and the greeting is thrown away.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
Operators must be able to enable or disable authentication without letting an attacker do the same. Authentication state learned for an IP address through an interface MAY be forgotten if that interface is administratively disabled, and implementations SHOULD let the state be shown and cleared through an authenticated channel.

The RFC recommends that all deployments use the TLV. Its strength depends on the algorithm, the key and a correct implementation. It confirms only that the packet came from a router with access to the key, not which specific originator sent it. Keys should be long and random, and management systems SHOULD accept hexadecimal key input. The RFC admits the mechanism is not perfect but says it raises the effort required for an attacker significantly without undue complexity.
sections.eli5: The secret proves the sender knows the password, not exactly who they are, so the password must be long and hard to guess.
